title: How To Handle A Student Who Complains About A Grade out-a-grade/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes between a student respectfully questioning a grade, which he says should be encouraged, and mere complaining aimed at guilting or pressuring a change, which requires a careful six-step response. The sequence runs from staying outwardly calm and simply listening, to deliberately delaying any reaction with 'let me do some research and get back to you,' to later delivering only the objective facts from a rubric, teaching the whole class the respectful way to raise a grade concern, enforcing any procedural violation separately, and finally reconnecting warmly with the student a day later to show there's no lingering grudge. He frames the goal as preserving a student's underlying drive to succeed while discouraging the disrespectful mode of complaining, closing with a reminder that classroom-management moments like this are opportunities to teach lessons that outlast the specific incident.
points: A distinction is drawn between respectful grade inquiry, which should be encouraged, and mere complaining meant to guilt or pressure a change.
The first response step is staying outwardly calm and simply listening without reacting or shutting the student down.
Delaying any substantive response with a line like 'let me do some research and get back to you' cools the interaction and reasserts authority.
Teaching the whole class the respectful way to raise a grade concern is used to prevent repeat incidents from other students too.
Reconnecting warmly with the student a day later — a fist bump or shared joke — signals there's no lingering grudge over the incident.
quotes: A student questioning a grade isn’t a problem. In fact, it should be encouraged. Inquiring why they received a particular grade shows initiative and the desire to do well.
Mere complaining, however, is not. Because it carries with it an element of rudeness and disrespect .

This response adds a level of seriousness to their charge while at the same time reminding them of your position as an authority. More importantly, it puts you in control and gives them time to cool off.
The way it works in this case is that you would teach your entire class how to respectfully inquire about a grade—when and how to approach you, what to say, how to be prepared, etc.
At some point, perhaps a day later, be sure to cruise by the student’s desk and give them a silent fist bump or share a joke and a smile to let them know that you don’t hold a grudge.
As teachers, we’re not just trying to get through each day, we’re endeavoring to instill skills and lessons that last a lifetime.
